summary: The note presents a series of dated vignettes (September–October 2023) showing how rituals and superstitions shape daily life across cultures, from morning altars in Mexico to evening customs in Peru and Norway. Each person's practice is tied to heritage, family, or hope for luck and protection. It concludes that these customs reflect a human desire for control, comprehension and comfort amid uncertainty.
one_line: Vignettes of people worldwide in autumn 2023 practicing daily rituals and superstitions, showing how customs provide meaning, identity, comfort and a sense of control.
key_facts: On September 3, 2023, Eliana Gonzalez of Oaxaca, Mexico, rises before dawn to prepare a small altar with marigolds and candles honoring her ancestors and whispers a prayer passed down through generations.

Aarav Mehta, an aspiring novelist in Mumbai, India, faces west toward success as his grandmother insisted, places a statue of Lord Ganesha on his desk to remove obstacles, and wears a dot of sandalwood paste on his forehead when writing (September 12, 2023).

Sofia Romano, a soccer player in Italy, loops her shoelaces three times before knotting them as a lucky charm taught by her father, and credits her winning goal on September 15, 2023 partly to this ritual.
Philip Thompson, a banker from London, England, never passes butter hand to hand, following a British superstition that doing so brings financial misfortune (September 20, 2023).
In China, not splitting a pear is a food ritual meant to avoid separation from loved ones.
Esra Yilmaz of Istanbul, Turkey, reads the grounds of her Turkish coffee to tell fortunes on September 24, 2023, a custom ingrained in Turkish culture.
Anna Rowland of Savannah, Georgia, picks up heads-up pennies on her afternoon stroll as signs of good luck.
On September 29, 2023, Kenyan storyteller Samuel Njoroge gathers local children to tell tales of mythical creatures and valiant ancestors that teach values, history and wisdom.
Oliver Chen of New York City honors his Taiwanese heritage by offering food and burning incense each evening for his ancestors, believing it invokes their protection.

On her wedding day, October 4, 2023, Maria Fernanda of Seville, Spain, wears something old, something new, something borrowed, and something blue, symbolizing continuity, optimism, borrowed happiness and fidelity.
On October 9, 2023, Hikaru Nakamura of Japan visits a local shrine to draw an Omikuji fortune-telling strip before launching his new business.
Lila Alvarado of Lima, Peru, turns her purse upside-down before bedtime (October 13, 2023) to keep family finances secure, following her grandmother's custom.
Erik Bergensen of Norway keeps all knives out of sight before sleeping, believing visible knives could invite unwanted spirits or disrupt dreams.
